slides.heading: A new political body in 1906
slides.body_md: Part 1 — the **background**, the **Simla Deputation**, the **founding at Dacca** and the **objectives**.

slides.narration: By the early nineteen hundreds the Indian National Congress was twenty years old. In December nineteen oh six a new political organisation was formed at Dacca: the All India Muslim League. In this part we look at the background to its formation, the deputation that met the Viceroy at Simla, the founding meeting itself, and the aims the League set for itself.

slides.narration: This timeline shows the main dates of the chapter. The college at Aligarh was founded in eighteen seventy-five and the Congress in eighteen eighty-five. Bengal was partitioned in nineteen oh five. The Simla Deputation met the Viceroy in October nineteen oh six, and the League was founded that December. Separate electorates came in nineteen oh nine, and the Lucknow Pact in nineteen sixteen.

slides.heading: Factors behind the League
slides.body_md: Historians link **several factors** with the League's formation; where views differ, learn both sides.

rows: British policy of "divide and rule" (nationalist view)
Encouraging separate interests so communities would not unite
Educational and economic backwardness
Sections of Muslims felt left behind in education and jobs
Influence of Sir Syed Ahmad Khan
Modern education at Aligarh; advice to keep away from the Congress
Partition of Bengal and the agitation against it
A Muslim-majority province some welcomed; fear of its undoing
Simla Deputation, October 1906
A favourable hearing encouraged a permanent body

visual.caption: Factors as listed in most ICSE lessons; give two sides where views differ.

slides.narration: Several factors are commonly linked with the founding of the League. Nationalists blamed a British policy of divide and rule. Sections of Muslims felt they lagged behind in education and jobs. Sir Syed Ahmad Khan's work at Aligarh shaped many leaders. The Partition of Bengal and the agitation against it mattered. And the Simla Deputation showed what an organised body could achieve.

slides.body_md: Under which Viceroy was Bengal partitioned?
slides.narration: The partition came in nineteen oh five. Which Viceroy carried it out?

slides.heading: The Partition of Bengal
slides.body_md: A **Muslim-majority** new province, and an agitation to undo it.

nodes.label: Eastern Bengal and Assam: a Muslim-majority province
Strong agitation to undo it (boycott, swadeshi)
These leaders feel the need for their own body

visual.alt: Flow: in 1905 Curzon divides Bengal, creating Eastern Bengal and Assam with a Muslim majority; some Muslim leaders welcome it; a strong agitation seeks to undo it; these leaders feel they need their own organisation
visual.caption: One link between 1905 and 1906.

slides.narration: In nineteen oh five Lord Curzon divided Bengal. The new province of Eastern Bengal and Assam had a Muslim majority, and some Muslim leaders welcomed it as an opportunity for their community. The strong agitation against the partition, with boycott and swadeshi, worried them. They began to feel that they needed an organisation of their own to protect what they saw as their interests.

slides.heading: Divide and rule, and backwardness
columns:
**"Divide and rule" (nationalist view)**

- Government accused of encouraging **separate interests**
- Aim, as critics saw it: keep communities from **uniting**

**Sense of backwardness**

- Sections of Muslims behind in **English education**
- Fewer **government jobs** and **professions**
- Wish for a body to **speak for** them
slides.narration: Two factors are often paired. Nationalists accused the government of divide and rule: encouraging separate interests so that communities would not unite against it. At the same time, sections of Muslims felt they had fallen behind in English education, government jobs and the professions, and wanted an organisation that would speak for them. Remember to present the divide and rule idea as a view.

slides.narration: Sir Syed Ahmad Khan founded the Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College at Aligarh in eighteen seventy-five to spread modern education among Muslims. He advised Muslims to keep away from the Congress at that stage and to concentrate on education. Many leaders of the next generation came from this background, which is why his work is often mentioned in the story of the League.

visual.alt: Table of facts about the Simla Deputation: October 1906, at Simla, led by Aga Khan III, met Viceroy Lord Minto, demanded separate electorates and fair representation in councils

slides.narration: In October nineteen oh six a group of Muslim leaders led by Aga Khan the Third met the Viceroy, Lord Minto, at Simla. They asked that Muslims be given separate representation in elected councils, in keeping with what they saw as their political importance. The Viceroy gave them a sympathetic hearing, which encouraged the same leaders to form a permanent body.

slides.narration: Leaders who had gathered at Dacca for the All India Muhammadan Educational Conference stayed on and, on the thirtieth of December nineteen oh six, founded the All India Muslim League. The meeting was hosted by Nawab Salimullah of Dacca. Aga Khan the Third, who had led the Simla Deputation, became its first President.

For example, the partition of nineteen oh five with the new Muslim-majority province, the sense of backwardness in education and jobs, and the Simla Deputation that encouraged organisation. Give each one a detail. If you mention divide and rule, present it as the nationalist view, not as a settled fact.

slides.heading: Objectives in 1906
slides.body_md: **Loyalty**, **political rights** and **harmony** (paraphrased).

nodes.label: Protect and advance Muslims' political rights
Place Muslims' needs before the government

visual.alt: Flow of the League's objectives in 1906: loyalty to the British government, protecting and advancing Muslims' political rights, placing their needs before the government, and preventing hostility towards other communities
visual.caption: Objectives at the founding (paraphrased).

slides.narration: At its founding the League set out three objectives. First, to promote loyalty among Muslims to the British government. Second, to protect and advance the political rights of Muslims and place their needs before the government. Third, to prevent hostility among Muslims towards other communities. Learn these in your own words; no exact wording is needed.

slides.heading: Quick check: an objective
slides.body_md: One of the first objectives was to promote ___ towards the British government.
slides.narration: The first objective concerned the League's attitude to the government. Which word completes it?

slides.heading: Worked example 2: factor or objective?
slides.body_md: Sort imagined statements into **causes** and **aims**.
bullets: A **factor** explains **why** the League was formed.
An **objective** states what the League **wanted to do**.
Check the tense: worries about the past or present are often factors; plans are aims.

rows: "We must keep good relations with the government."
Objective (loyalty)
"Our young people lag behind in colleges and offices."
Factor (backwardness)
"The protests in Calcutta may undo our new province."
Factor (partition)
"We should speak for our community's needs."
Objective (political rights)

visual.alt: Worked example table sorting four imagined statements: keeping good relations with the government and speaking for the community's needs are objectives; lagging behind in colleges and fear of undoing the new province are factors
visual.caption: Imagined statements written by SOYL. Ask: is it a cause, or an aim?

slides.narration: Exam questions often mix up factors and objectives, so practise telling them apart. In these imagined statements, keeping good relations with the government is an objective, and so is speaking for the community's needs. Lagging behind in colleges and offices is a factor, and so is the fear that protests might undo the new province.

slides.body_md: Simla (October) came **before** Dacca (December).

slides.narration: To sum up Part One. Nationalists blamed divide and rule; sections of Muslims felt left behind; Aligarh shaped many leaders. Its aims were loyalty, the protection of political rights, and harmony with other communities.

slides.heading: From Dacca to Lucknow

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: separate electorates in 1909, the annulment of the partition in 1911, the League's new aim in 1913, the Lucknow Pact of 1916 and its impact
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: In Part Two we follow the League over the next ten years. Separate electorates came in nineteen oh nine. The partition of Bengal was undone in nineteen eleven. In nineteen thirteen the League adopted a new aim. And in nineteen sixteen it agreed on a joint scheme with the Congress at Lucknow. We end by weighing the impact of that agreement.

slides.heading: Separate electorates, 1909
slides.body_md: The **Indian Councils Act, 1909** (Morley-Minto Reforms) gave Muslims **separate electorates**.

rows: All voters of a constituency choose the member together
Only voters of one community choose members reserved for it
Candidates appeal to every community
Candidates appeal to their own community

visual.alt: Table comparing joint and separate electorates: in a joint electorate all voters choose together and candidates appeal to everyone; in a separate electorate only one community's voters choose members reserved for it
visual.caption: Separate electorates came with the Indian Councils Act, 1909.

slides.narration: The Indian Councils Act of nineteen oh nine, known as the Morley-Minto Reforms, enlarged the legislative councils. It also gave Muslims separate electorates: in seats reserved for Muslims, only Muslim voters chose the member. This met the main demand of the Simla Deputation. Compare it with a joint electorate, in which all voters of a constituency choose together.

slides.heading: How the League changed
slides.body_md: From **loyalty** in 1906 to **cooperation** in 1916.

visual.alt: Flow of how the League changed: loyalty and separate representation in 1906, separate electorates won in 1909, trust shaken by the annulment of 1911, the aim of self-government in 1913, and the joint scheme with the Congress in 1916
visual.caption: From loyalty to cooperation.

slides.narration: The League changed over these years. In nineteen eleven the partition of Bengal was annulled, which disappointed leaders who had trusted the government. Younger leaders favoured working with the Congress. In nineteen thirteen the League adopted the goal of self-government suited to India, an aim close to that of the Congress. By nineteen sixteen the two could agree on a joint scheme.

sections.heading: 1. Background: factors commonly linked with the League
sections.body_md:
- **"Divide and rule":** nationalists argued that the government encouraged **separate interests** among communities so that they would not unite against British rule. Present this as a **view**.
- **Backwardness:** sections of Muslims felt they lagged behind in **English education**, **government jobs** and the **professions**.
- **Sir Syed Ahmad Khan:** founded the **Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College, Aligarh (1875)**; urged modern education and advised Muslims to keep away from the **Congress** at that stage.

key_terms.definition_md: A policy, as nationalists described it, of encouraging differences between communities so that they would not unite.

sections.heading: 2. The Partition of Bengal and the Simla Deputation
sections.body_md:
- **1905:** **Lord Curzon** partitioned Bengal; the new province of **Eastern Bengal and Assam** had a **Muslim majority**, and some Muslim leaders welcomed it.
- The strong **agitation** against the partition (boycott, swadeshi) made these leaders feel they needed their **own organisation**.
- **Simla Deputation, October 1906:** led by **Aga Khan III**, met the Viceroy **Lord Minto**; asked for **separate electorates** and fair representation in councils. The sympathetic hearing encouraged the founding of a permanent body.

sections.heading: 4. Objectives of the League (paraphrased)
sections.body_md:
1. To promote **loyalty** among Muslims to the **British government**.
2. To defend and promote the **political rights** of Muslims and make their **needs** known to the government.
3. To prevent the growth among Muslims of **hostility towards other communities**.

**Separate electorates:** the **Indian Councils Act, 1909** (Morley-Minto Reforms) enlarged the councils and gave Muslims separate electorates.

**Change by 1913:** the **annulment of the partition (1911)** shook trust in the government; younger leaders such as **Muhammad Ali Jinnah** (joined the League in **1913**) favoured cooperation; the League adopted the goal of **self-government suited to India**.

sections.heading: 5. The Lucknow Pact, 1916
sections.body_md:
- **When and where:** **December 1916**, **Lucknow**, where both the **Congress** and the **League** held their sessions.
- **Parties:** the **Indian National Congress** and the **All India Muslim League**; leaders most associated: **Bal Gangadhar Tilak** and **Muhammad Ali Jinnah**. **Ambika Charan Mazumdar** presided over the Congress session.
- **Congress reunion:** the **Moderates** and **Assertive Nationalists**, split at **Surat (1907)**, came together again at the same session.
- **Main terms (paraphrased):** a **joint demand for self-government**; **enlarged councils** with an **elected majority**; **separate electorates accepted** by the Congress; **Muslim seat shares fixed province by province**.

sections.heading: 6. Impact of the Lucknow Pact
sections.body_md:
- **Unity:** the two main organisations made **one demand**, showing **Hindu-Muslim cooperation**.
- **A stronger Congress:** the reunion meant the Congress spoke with **one voice**.
- **Pressure for self-government** during the **First World War**.
- **Long-term debate:** some historians argue that accepting **separate electorates** entrenched politics by **community**; others see it as the **necessary price** of unity in 1916. Give both views.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Giving 1905 or 1909 as the year the League was founded (it was **30 December 1906**).
- Confusing **Nawab Salimullah** (host) with **Aga Khan III** (first President).
- Saying independence was a 1906 objective.
- Treating the Congress **reunion** and the **Pact** as the same event.
- Saying the Congress **rejected** separate electorates in 1916 (it **accepted** them).
- Presenting "divide and rule" as settled fact rather than a view.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: one correct option or term.
- 2 marks: two distinct points.
- 10-mark questions in 3 + 3 + 4 parts: one point per mark; the 4-mark part often asks for impact or a balanced view.

questions.stem_md: In which year was the All India Muslim League formed at a meeting held in Dacca?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** 1906. The League was formed on 30 December 1906 at Dacca. The Partition of Bengal was in 1905, the Morley-Minto Reforms in 1909 and the Lucknow Pact in 1916.

questions.stem_md: In which city did the meeting that founded the Muslim League take place?

options.text_md: Aligarh
Lucknow
Lahore
Dacca (Dhaka)

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Dacca (Dhaka). The League was founded at Dacca, during a session of the All India Muhammadan Educational Conference. Aligarh was the centre of Sir Syed Ahmad Khan's college, and the Pact of 1916 was signed at Lucknow.

questions.stem_md: The Muslim League was set up at the end of the annual session of which body held at Dacca in December 1906?

options.text_md: The All India Muhammadan Educational Conference
The Indian National Congress
The Indian Association
The Imperial Legislative Council

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The All India Muhammadan Educational Conference. Leaders who had gathered for the All India Muhammadan Educational Conference at Dacca decided to form the League. The Congress, the Indian Association and the Legislative Council were separate bodies.

questions.stem_md: Who is remembered as the first President of the All India Muslim League?

options.text_md: Muhammad Ali Jinnah
Nawab Salimullah
Aga Khan III
Lord Minto

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Aga Khan III. Aga Khan III, who had also led the Simla Deputation, was chosen as the League's first President. Jinnah joined the League later (1913); Salimullah hosted the Dacca meeting; Minto was the Viceroy.

questions.stem_md: In October 1906 a group of Muslim leaders met Lord Minto at Simla. What was the main demand of this Simla Deputation?

options.text_md: Immediate independence for India
Annulment of the Partition of Bengal
Separate representation for Muslims in elected councils
Abolition of the Arms Act

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Separate representation for Muslims in elected councils. The Deputation asked for separate electorates and representation for Muslims in councils. It did not ask for independence; it did not seek the annulment of the partition, which many of its members welcomed; the Arms Act was not its subject.

questions.stem_md: Which Viceroy received the Simla Deputation in 1906?

options.text_md: Lord Minto
Lord Curzon
Lord Ripon
Lord Hardinge

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Lord Minto. Lord Minto, Viceroy from 1905 to 1910, received the Deputation. Curzon partitioned Bengal in 1905; Ripon belongs to the 1880s; Hardinge was Viceroy when the partition was annulled in 1911.

questions.stem_md: Nationalist writers often say that British "divide and rule" helped bring about the Muslim League. What does the phrase mean in this context?

options.text_md: Dividing India into provinces for easier tax collection
Splitting the army into regiments by region
Dividing power equally between the Viceroy and the princes
Encouraging differences between communities so that they would not unite against British rule

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Encouraging differences between communities so that they would not unite against British rule. The phrase describes a policy, as nationalists saw it, of encouraging separate interests among communities so that they would not unite against the government. The other options describe administrative arrangements, not this idea.

questions.stem_md: Why did the agitation against the Partition of Bengal worry some Muslim leaders of eastern Bengal?

options.text_md: They wanted Bengal to be ruled directly from London
They felt the new province, with a Muslim majority, offered them better opportunities, and its undoing could harm their interests
They opposed all forms of education
They had already joined the Congress in large numbers

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** They felt the new province, with a Muslim majority, offered them better opportunities, and its undoing could harm their interests. The new province of Eastern Bengal and Assam had a Muslim majority, and some Muslim leaders saw it as an opportunity; the agitation to undo it seemed to them to go against their interests. The other options are not historical.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is usually listed as a factor behind the formation of the Muslim League?

options.text_md: The feeling that sections of Muslims lagged behind in modern education and government jobs
The success of the Lucknow Pact
The failure of the Cripps Mission
The Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The feeling that sections of Muslims lagged behind in modern education and government jobs. A sense of educational and economic backwardness among sections of Muslims is a commonly taught factor. The Lucknow Pact (1916), the Cripps Mission (1942) and the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms (1919) all came after 1906.

questions.stem_md: Sir Syed Ahmad Khan, founder of the college at Aligarh, is often mentioned in the background to the Muslim League. Which view is usually associated with him?

options.text_md: That Muslims should lead an armed revolt
That Muslims should concentrate on modern education and keep away from the Congress for the time being
That English education was harmful to Muslims
That the Congress should be the only voice of all Indians

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** That Muslims should concentrate on modern education and keep away from the Congress for the time being. Sir Syed promoted modern education through the Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College (1875) and advised Muslims to stay away from the Congress at that stage. He did not call for revolt, he favoured English education, and he did not see the Congress as speaking for Muslims.

questions.stem_md: The Indian Councils Act of 1909 is linked to the demands of the Simla Deputation. What did it introduce?

options.text_md: Universal adult franchise
Full self-government for India
Separate electorates for Muslims
An Indian Viceroy

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Separate electorates for Muslims. The Morley-Minto Reforms of 1909 gave Muslims separate electorates, as the Deputation had asked. Adult franchise came with the Constitution of 1950; self-government and an Indian Viceroy were not part of the 1909 Act.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The Simla Deputation of 1906 is regarded as a step towards the formation of the Muslim League.

**Reason (R):** The Deputation showed Muslim leaders that an organised body could press their demands on the government.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: (A) is true and (R) is false.
(A) is false and (R) is true.
Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Both are true, and R explains A: the favourable hearing at Simla encouraged the same leaders to set up a permanent organisation a few weeks later at Dacca.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Some Muslim leaders of eastern Bengal supported the Partition of Bengal of 1905.

**Reason (R):** The Partition of Bengal created a new province with a Hindu majority.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: (A) is true and (R) is false.
(A) is false and (R) is true.
Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** A is true. R is false: the new province of Eastern Bengal and Assam had a Muslim majority, which is why some Muslim leaders welcomed it.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The Muslim League was founded in the same year as the Indian National Congress.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** False. The Congress was founded in 1885 and the Muslim League in 1906, twenty-one years later.

questions.stem_md: The All India Muslim League was founded on 30 December 1906 at ___.
questions.solution_md: It was founded at Dacca (now Dhaka).

questions.stem_md: Mention any two factors that led to the formation of the Muslim League in 1906.
questions.solution_md: Any two recognised factors.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. The British policy of **"divide and rule"**, as nationalists saw it, which encouraged separate political interests.
2. A feeling of **educational and economic backwardness** among sections of Muslims. (Also: the reaction to the **anti-partition agitation**, or the **Simla Deputation**.)

questions.stem_md: Give two facts about the Simla Deputation of 1906.
questions.solution_md: Leader and Viceroy; main demand.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. It was led by **Aga Khan III** and met the Viceroy **Lord Minto** at **Simla** in **October 1906**.
2. It asked for **separate electorates** and fair **representation** for Muslims in councils.

questions.stem_md: How did the Partition of Bengal and the movement against it influence the formation of the Muslim League?
questions.solution_md: The new province; reaction to the agitation.

answer.model_answer_md: The partition created **Eastern Bengal and Assam**, a **Muslim-majority** province that some Muslim leaders welcomed. The strong **agitation to undo it** made them feel they needed their **own organisation** to protect what they saw as their interests.

marking_scheme.step: Agitation leads to need for own body

questions.stem_md: State two ways in which Sir Syed Ahmad Khan's work is linked to the background of the Muslim League.
questions.solution_md: Education; political advice.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. He founded the **Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College** at **Aligarh (1875)**, spreading **modern education** among Muslims; many later League leaders came from this background.
2. He advised Muslims to **stay away from the Congress** at that stage, encouraging a **separate political path**.

questions.stem_md: Explain three factors that historians commonly link with the founding of the Muslim League.
questions.solution_md: Three distinct factors, each explained.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **British policy:** nationalists argue that the government encouraged **separate interests** among communities ("divide and rule").
2. **Backwardness:** sections of Muslims felt they lagged in **modern education** and **government jobs**, and wanted a body to speak for them.
3. **Partition of Bengal:** some Muslim leaders welcomed the **Muslim-majority** new province and saw the agitation against it as a threat, which led them to organise.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following was one of the objectives of the Muslim League at its formation in 1906?

options.text_md: To demand complete independence at once
To merge with the Indian National Congress
To boycott all British goods
To promote loyalty among Muslims towards the British government

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** To promote loyalty among Muslims towards the British government. At first the League aimed to promote loyalty to the British government among Muslims. Complete independence, merger with the Congress and boycott were not its aims in 1906.

questions.stem_md: According to its stated aims of 1906, how did the League intend to protect the political rights of Muslims?

options.text_md: By organising armed resistance
By refusing to take part in any council
By asking the British to leave India
By representing their needs and aspirations to the government

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** By representing their needs and aspirations to the government. The League planned to protect Muslims' political rights by placing their needs and aspirations before the government. It did not plan armed resistance or a boycott of councils, and it did not ask the British to leave in 1906.

questions.stem_md: One aim of the League in 1906 was to prevent hostility among Muslims towards other communities. What does this aim suggest about the League's original approach?

options.text_md: It wanted to keep Muslims out of politics
It planned to take over the Congress
It meant to protect Muslim interests without encouraging ill will towards others
It opposed all contact with other communities

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** It meant to protect Muslim interests without encouraging ill will towards others. The aim shows that the League presented itself as a defender of Muslim interests while also, in principle, discouraging hostility towards other communities. The other options contradict its stated aims.

questions.stem_md: By 1913 the League had changed its aims. Which new goal did it adopt?

options.text_md: A separate country for Muslims
Self-government suited to India, in cooperation with other communities
Rule by the princes
Withdrawal from all elections

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Self-government suited to India, in cooperation with other communities. In 1913 the League adopted the goal of self-government suitable to India, which brought it closer to the Congress and paved the way for the Lucknow Pact. A separate country was not demanded at this time.

questions.stem_md: Which of these was NOT among the objectives of the Muslim League when it was founded?

options.text_md: Ending British rule through mass non-cooperation
Promoting loyalty to the British government
Protecting the political rights of Muslims
Preventing hostility towards other communities

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Ending British rule through mass non-cooperation. Mass non-cooperation belongs to the Gandhian movements after 1920. The other three were among the League's stated aims in 1906.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** In 1906 the Muslim League stated loyalty to the British government as one of its aims.

**Reason (R):** The Muslim League was founded at Dacca.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: (A) is true and (R) is false.
(A) is false and (R) is true.
Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Both statements are true, but R (where it was founded) does not explain A (why it stated loyalty as an aim).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The Muslim League never changed its aims between 1906 and 1916.

**Reason (R):** In 1913 the League adopted the goal of self-government suited to India.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: (A) is true and (R) is false.
(A) is false and (R) is true.
Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** A is false because the League did change its aims. R is true: in 1913 it adopted the goal of self-government, which made the 1916 Pact with the Congress possible.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Complete independence from Britain was one of the original objectives of the Muslim League in 1906.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** False. Its original objectives included loyalty to the British government and the protection of Muslims' political rights; independence was not among them.

questions.stem_md: State any two objectives of the Muslim League at the time of its formation.
questions.solution_md: Any two of the three objectives.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. To promote **loyalty** among Muslims to the **British government**.
2. To **protect and advance** the **political rights** of Muslims and place their needs before the government. (Also: to prevent **hostility** among Muslims towards other communities.)

questions.stem_md: Give two reasons why the League's outlook changed between 1906 and 1913.
questions.solution_md: Annulment; new leadership and goals.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. The **annulment of the Partition of Bengal (1911)** disappointed many League leaders who had trusted the government.
2. Younger leaders, including **Muhammad Ali Jinnah** (who joined in **1913**), favoured working with the Congress for **self-government**.

marking_scheme.step: New leaders and goal of self-government

questions.stem_md: Explain the three objectives the Muslim League set out for itself in 1906.
questions.solution_md: Three objectives, each explained.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Loyalty:** to encourage among Muslims a feeling of **loyalty** to the British government and remove misunderstandings about its intentions.
2. **Political rights:** to **protect and advance** the political rights of Muslims and present their **needs** to the government in moderate language.
3. **Harmony:** to prevent the growth among Muslims of **hostility** towards other communities, without harming the first two aims.

questions.stem_md: Between which two organisations was the Lucknow Pact agreed?

options.text_md: The Congress and the British government
The Indian National Congress and the All India Muslim League
The Muslim League and the princely states
The Moderates and the Assertive Nationalists

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The Indian National Congress and the All India Muslim League. The Pact was an agreement between the Congress and the Muslim League. The Moderates and Assertive Nationalists reunited within the Congress at the same session, but that was not the Pact itself.

questions.stem_md: Which pair of leaders is most closely associated with negotiating the Lucknow Pact?

options.text_md: Gopal Krishna Gokhale and Aga Khan III
Dadabhai Naoroji and Sir Syed Ahmad Khan
Mahatma Gandhi and Maulana Azad
Bal Gangadhar Tilak and Muhammad Ali Jinnah

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Bal Gangadhar Tilak and Muhammad Ali Jinnah. Tilak, for the Congress, and Jinnah, for the League, are the leaders most associated with the Pact. Gokhale had died in 1915; Naoroji and Sir Syed belong to an earlier phase; Gandhi was not yet the leading figure in 1916.

questions.stem_md: Which other important event took place within the Congress at its Lucknow session of 1916?

options.text_md: The Moderates and the Assertive Nationalists came together again
The Congress split into two groups
The Congress adopted complete independence as its goal
The Congress decided to boycott all elections

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The Moderates and the Assertive Nationalists came together again. The two groups that had split at Surat in 1907 reunited at Lucknow in 1916. The Congress adopted complete independence only in 1929, at Lahore.

questions.stem_md: Under the Lucknow Pact, what did the Congress agree to regarding the way Muslims would elect their representatives?

options.text_md: It insisted on joint electorates only
It asked for elections to be abolished
It accepted separate electorates for Muslims
It left the matter to the princes

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** It accepted separate electorates for Muslims. The Congress accepted separate electorates for Muslims, with seat shares fixed province by province, in return for a joint demand for self-government.

questions.stem_md: What common demand did the Congress and the League place before the government through the Lucknow Pact?

options.text_md: Immediate independence by force
Restoration of the Mughal empire
Self-government for India, with larger elected councils
Separate countries for each community

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Self-government for India, with larger elected councils. The two bodies jointly demanded self-government, with enlarged legislative councils having a majority of elected members. The other options were not part of the Pact.

questions.stem_md: Why is the Lucknow Pact often described as a high point of cooperation in the national movement?

options.text_md: The Congress and the League made a joint demand, and the two Congress groups reunited at the same time
It ended British rule in India
It abolished separate electorates
It was signed by the Viceroy

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The Congress and the League made a joint demand, and the two Congress groups reunited at the same time. The Pact brought the Congress and the League together in a common demand, and it coincided with the reunion of Moderates and Assertive Nationalists. questions.stem_md:
Answer the following about the formation of the Muslim League.

(i) When and where was the Muslim League founded, and who were two leaders associated with its founding? **[3]**
(ii) What was the Simla Deputation, and what did it ask for? **[3]**
(iii) Explain how the Partition of Bengal and the agitation against it contributed to the formation of the League. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Date, place, leaders; the Deputation; the partition link.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) It was founded on **30 December 1906** at **Dacca**, at a meeting held during the **All India Muhammadan Educational Conference**. **Nawab Salimullah** of Dacca hosted it, and **Aga Khan III** became its first **President**.

(ii) In **October 1906** a group of Muslim leaders led by **Aga Khan III** met the Viceroy **Lord Minto** at **Simla**. They asked for **separate electorates** and for Muslim representation in councils in keeping with their political importance.

(iii) **Curzon's** partition (**1905**) created **Eastern Bengal and Assam**, a **Muslim-majority** province that some Muslim leaders welcomed as an opportunity. The strong **agitation** to undo it, using methods such as **boycott and swadeshi**, made these leaders feel that their interests needed a **separate organisation**, and the favourable reply at Simla encouraged them to form one at Dacca.

questions.stem_md:
Answer the following about the background to the Muslim League.

(i) Explain what nationalists meant when they blamed British "divide and rule" for the rise of separate politics. **[3]**
(ii) How did Sir Syed Ahmad Khan's work and views form part of the background? **[3]**
(iii) Explain how a sense of educational and economic backwardness among sections of Muslims led to the demand for a separate organisation. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Divide and rule; Sir Syed; backwardness.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) Nationalists argued that the government **encouraged differences** between communities, for example through **separate concessions** and by favouring **separate representation**, so that Indians would not **unite** against British rule.

(ii) Sir Syed founded the **Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College**, Aligarh (**1875**), to spread **modern education** among Muslims. He advised Muslims to keep away from the **Congress** at that stage, which encouraged a **separate political outlook** among the educated class he influenced.

(iii) Sections of Muslims felt they had fallen behind in **English education**, **government jobs** and **professions**. Their leaders believed that their interests would be overlooked in bodies dominated by others, so they wanted an **organisation of their own** to place their **needs** before the government and secure **representation**.

questions.stem_md:
Answer the following about the Muslim League's aims.

(i) State the three objectives of the Muslim League at its formation. **[3]**
(ii) How did the Indian Councils Act of 1909 respond to the League's demands? **[3]**
(iii) Explain how and why the League's aims changed by 1913. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Three objectives; the 1909 Act; change of aims.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) To promote **loyalty** among Muslims to the **British government**; to **protect and advance** the **political rights** of Muslims and represent their needs; and to prevent **hostility** among Muslims towards **other communities**.

(ii) The **Morley-Minto Reforms** (Indian Councils Act, **1909**) **enlarged** the legislative councils and gave Muslims **separate electorates**, in which only Muslim voters chose Muslim members, meeting the main demand of the Simla Deputation.

(iii) The **annulment of the Partition of Bengal in 1911** disappointed League leaders who had trusted the government, and younger leaders such as **Jinnah** favoured **cooperation** with the Congress. In **1913** the League adopted the goal of **self-government suited to India**, which brought it close to the Congress and prepared the ground for **Lucknow (1916)**.

questions.solution_md: Who, when, where; terms; immediate impact.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) It was agreed in **December 1916** at **Lucknow** between the **Indian National Congress** and the **All India Muslim League**; **Bal Gangadhar Tilak** and **Muhammad Ali Jinnah** are the leaders most associated with it.

(ii) A **joint demand for self-government**; **enlarged councils** with a **majority of elected members**; and the Congress's **acceptance of separate electorates**, with **seat shares for Muslims fixed province by province**.

(iii) It showed **Hindu-Muslim unity** and gave the national movement a **common programme**. The same session saw the **reunion** of the **Moderates and Assertive Nationalists**, so the Congress spoke with one voice, and the **joint demand** for self-government added pressure on the British government during the **First World War**.

questions.stem_md:
Answer the following about the significance of the Lucknow Pact.

(i) Explain three developments that made agreement between the Congress and the League possible in 1916. **[3]**
(ii) Why is the Pact regarded as a landmark of cooperation? **[3]**
(iii) Present one argument for and one argument against the Congress's acceptance of separate electorates, and give your own reasoned view. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Developments; landmark; balanced evaluation.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) The **annulment of the partition (1911)**; the League's adoption of **self-government** as its aim (**1913**); and leaders such as **Jinnah**, who belonged to **both** bodies, together with the **reunion** of the Congress groups.

(ii) For the first time the **two main organisations** agreed on a **common scheme**; it showed that **communities could cooperate**; and it gave the demand for **self-government** wider support.

(iii) **For:** it was a practical **compromise** that won the League's trust and made a **united demand** possible. **Against:** it **recognised community-based representation**, which critics see as having **long-term consequences**. A balanced view may say it achieved **short-term unity** at the cost of accepting a principle that later proved **divisive**; any reasoned judgement earns credit.

questions.passage_md:
**Diary of an imagined student delegate from Patna, Dacca, December 1906**

The education conference ended today, but many of the elders stayed on. Our host, a nobleman of this city, spoke of how the new province had opened schools and offices to people like us, and of how the protests in Calcutta might take it all away. An older delegate reminded us that a group had already gone to Simla in the autumn and been heard kindly. By evening it was settled: we would have a body of our own, to speak for our community to the government, to stay on good terms with it, and to live at peace with our neighbours.

**Letter from an imagined lawyer in Lucknow to his brother in Madras, January 1917**

Brother, you would not have believed the scenes last week. The two old rival groups of the Congress sat side by side as if Surat had never happened. Across the city, the League met too, and by the end the two bodies had agreed on one plan to put before the government: more elected members, a real share in ruling, and an arrangement on seats that our Muslim friends had long asked for. Some of my colleagues say this last point will cost us dearly one day; others say there could be no agreement without it. I do not yet know who is right.

questions.stem_md: Under which Viceroy was Bengal partitioned in 1905?

options.text_md: Lord Curzon
Lord Minto
Lord Ripon
Lord Lytton

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Lord Curzon. Lord Curzon carried out the partition in 1905. Minto followed him; Ripon and Lytton belong to the 1870s and 1880s.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The Simla Deputation met the Viceroy after the Muslim League had been founded at Dacca.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** False. The Deputation met Lord Minto in October 1906; the League was founded later, on 30 December 1906.

questions.stem_md: One of the first objectives of the Muslim League was to promote ___ among Muslims towards the British government.
questions.solution_md: Promoting loyalty to the British government was one of its first objectives.

questions.stem_md: Why was Muhammad Ali Jinnah well placed to help bring about the Lucknow Pact?

options.text_md: He was the Viceroy's adviser
He was a member of both the Congress and the Muslim League at the time
He had founded the League at Dacca
He opposed self-government

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** He was a member of both the Congress and the Muslim League at the time. Jinnah, who had joined the League in 1913 while remaining in the Congress, could act as a bridge between the two. He was not the Viceroy's adviser, did not found the League, and supported self-government.

questions.stem_md: In which city did the Congress and the League hold their sessions in December 1916, where they agreed on a joint scheme?

options.text_md: Surat
Calcutta
Lucknow
Dacca

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Lucknow. Both bodies met at Lucknow in December 1916. Surat (1907) saw the Congress split; Dacca saw the League's founding.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The British Viceroy was one of the parties that signed the Lucknow Pact.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** False. The Pact was an agreement between two Indian organisations, the Congress and the Muslim League; the government was not a party to it.

questions.stem_md: An imagined pamphlet printed in Dacca in 1906 complains that young men of the community find few places in colleges and government offices. It asks that the community's needs be put directly before the government, and it warns members that joining the agitation against the new province would risk the small gains made so far. Which inference about the writer's approach is best supported?

options.text_md: He wants the partition annulled at once so that Bengal is reunited
He believes that the community is already well represented in colleges and offices
He wants the community to join the Congress in demanding complete independence
He believes that the community is better served by pressing its own needs on the government than by joining the Congress-led agitation

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** He believes that the community is better served by pressing its own needs on the government than by joining the Congress-led agitation. The pamphlet lists a grievance (few places), asks for direct representation to the government and warns against joining the agitation, so the writer favours a separate, community-centred approach to the government. Wanting the partition annulled contradicts the warning, he complains of too few places so he cannot think the community well represented, and complete independence is not mentioned and was not a League aim in 1906.

questions.stem_md: At an imagined League meeting of 1907, a member proposes that the League join a campaign of public protest against a government decision. Which of the League's three objectives of 1906 would an opposing speaker most directly cite?

options.text_md: Protecting and advancing the political rights of Muslims
Preventing hostility towards other communities
Demanding self-government for India
Encouraging loyalty to the British government

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Encouraging loyalty to the British government. A campaign of protest against the government cuts across the objective of loyalty, so the opponent would cite that. The aims of protecting political rights and preventing hostility do not conflict with a protest, and self-government was not an objective of 1906 (it was adopted only in 1913).

questions.stem_md: In an imagined province, Muslims are a small minority of voters. A councillor explains that, under the Lucknow Pact, the share of seats for Muslims has been settled in advance. What is the most direct effect of this arrangement in his province?

options.text_md: Muslim voters take part in joint electorates with all other voters
The community can choose members for every seat in the council
The community is assured of a fixed share of the elected seats, whatever its numbers in an open contest
Seats for all other communities are abolished

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The community is assured of a fixed share of the elected seats, whatever its numbers in an open contest. Seat shares fixed in advance, with separate electorates, assure a minority community of its share whether or not it could win it in an open contest. The Pact kept separate electorates rather than joint ones, it did not let one community choose every member, and it did not abolish seats for others.

questions.stem_md: An imagined Congress delegate says in 1912, "Our party agreed to separate electorates, so we cannot object to this reserved seat." Which correction to his statement is best?

options.text_md: The arrangement was created by the Lucknow Pact, so no reserved seat could exist in 1912
The arrangement dates from 1909, but the Congress accepted it only in 1916, so in 1912 it had not yet agreed
Separate electorates were first demanded by the Congress in 1906
Muslim voters used joint electorates until 1916, so no seat could be reserved in 1912

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The arrangement dates from 1909, but the Congress accepted it only in 1916, so in 1912 it had not yet agreed. Separate electorates were introduced by the Indian Councils Act of 1909, so a reserved seat in 1912 is possible; but the Congress accepted the principle only in the Lucknow Pact of 1916. The other options misplace the dates: the Pact did not create the arrangement, the Congress did not demand it in 1906, and joint electorates were not used by Muslim voters after 1909.

questions.stem_md: In 1906 an imagined League member urged loyalty to the government; in 1914 an imagined League speaker calls for self-government, to be won together with other communities. Which pair of developments best explains the change?

options.text_md: The annulment of the partition in 1911 shook trust in the government, and younger leaders such as Jinnah, who joined in 1913, favoured working with the Congress
The Simla Deputation was received by the Viceroy in 1906, and the Indian Councils Act of 1909 introduced separate electorates
The founding of the Congress in 1885 and of the Aligarh college in 1875
The Lucknow Pact and the reunion of the Congress in 1916

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The annulment of the partition in 1911 shook trust in the government, and younger leaders such as Jinnah, who joined in 1913, favoured working with the Congress. The change had to be caused by events before 1914 that weakened trust in the government and favoured cooperation with others: the annulment of the partition (1911) and the arrival of leaders such as Jinnah (1913). The Deputation and the 1909 Act would, if anything, have strengthened trust in the government; 1885 and 1875 are too early to explain a change of 1913; and the Pact and reunion of 1916 came after the speech.

questions.stem_md: An imagined League member writes in 1912 that he trusts the government less than he did in 1906, although separate electorates were granted in 1909. Which reading best explains why the decision of 1911 about Bengal weighed more with him than that gain?

options.text_md: The decision of 1911 ended separate electorates, which he valued most
Leaders who had welcomed the eastern province saw its undoing as a sign that the government would give way to agitation
The decision of 1911 moved the capital to Calcutta and so away from Delhi
The decision of 1911 made the League illegal in Bengal

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Leaders who had welcomed the eastern province saw its undoing as a sign that the government would give way to agitation. Annulling the partition in 1911 disappointed those who had welcomed the new province and suggested that agitation could change government decisions, so it weighed more with him than the 1909 gain. The decision did not end separate electorates, the capital moved from Calcutta to Delhi (not the reverse), and the League was not made illegal.

questions.stem_md: An imagined delegate at Lucknow in 1916 notes that leaders who had quarrelled and parted at Surat now sit side by side, while the League meets in the same city. Which statement best explains why this was possible in 1916 but not in 1907?

options.text_md: The Congress had given up its demand for self-government, so there was nothing left to quarrel over
The Viceroy had ordered the two groups to unite and the League to attend
The Surat Split had been a misunderstanding about the venue, which was cleared up in 1916
Tilak was free again after his years in Mandalay, and with the League also seeking self-government a common programme made unity more useful than the old dispute over methods

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Tilak was free again after his years in Mandalay, and with the League also seeking self-government a common programme made unity more useful than the old dispute over methods. By 1916 a leading Assertive leader, Tilak, was free again (he was released in 1914), and the League had adopted the goal of self-government (1913), so a joint programme made reunion attractive. The Congress had not given up self-government, the Viceroy was not involved in the Congress's affairs, and the split had been about goals and methods, not a mere misunderstanding.

questions.stem_md: At Lucknow in 1916 an imagined Congress delegate objects: "Why should we accept seats fixed in advance for one community?" Give two points that a supporter of the Pact could make in reply.
questions.solution_md: Two points in reply, each tied to a term of the Pact.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Trust:** accepting **separate electorates** and **fixed seat shares** answered the League's main worry about representation and built **trust**.
2. **Strength:** in return the League joined a **joint demand for self-government**, which would weigh more with the government than separate demands.

Joint demand gives a stronger case for self-government
